chapter: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
title: Ivie's Chicken Shack
summary: Ivie Anderson and husband Mark Neal ran a popular food-only restaurant at Vernon and Central, which grew into a housing development.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Tell me about Ivie's Chicken Shack. That was on the corner of Vernon and Central Avenue. Is that right?
Yes. Uh-huh.
WILLARD
And did Ivie Anderson own it?
Yes. She owned it, and she had a friend that took very good care of it, was a very good shopper for meats and things like that, and it flourished, and from there
they built this housing area. I forget exactly where it is, but it's over there between San Pedro and that area.
What, the Nielanders? (Inaudible.)
Yeah, that was the name of it, yes.
On East 41st Place (inaudible).
Somewhere along in there. Yeah.
Was her husband at one time Mark Neal?
Mark Neal, yes.
And they also ran Ivie's Chicken Shack.
Yes, uh-huh.
And I have heard that it was a very popular place for show people.
Oh, abso -- they had very good food, number one, and then after work, you know, they'd come from the clubs and places where they worked and congregate there for food. They served nothing but food.
There was never any entertainment.
No, oh no. Just small restaurant like place.
What year was that, or what year is there --
Oh, gee. I can't imagine. I know she was in Jam for Joy out here in the forty -- early forties, so it had to be in that era. Of course there were all kinds of

small clubs up and down the Avenue where people went. Most of them were after-hours supper clubs, mostly, or after-hour spots, and most of them were too small, or being in houses, they would make too much noise if they had entertainment, so they couldn't have any more than, if any at all, just a piano player.
